newsitem.title: USA: US mayors call for more flexibility in welfare law.
newsitem.headline: US mayors call for more flexibility in welfare law.

text.p: U.S mayors Wednesday called for more flexibility in implementing a broad welfare reform law and warned some cities could face disaster without beefed up training and education programs to move people to work.

Speaking after the first meeting of a task force on welfare reform, put together by the U.S. Conference of Mayors, a group of mostly Democratic city executives said the law fell far short of what was needed to prepare recipients for jobs.

They said there was no consensus about the strategy cities should pursue in coming days. One said the mayors' meetings with congressional and White House officials Tuesday made World War II look like a small-scale domestic dispute.
"There are some people who say it will not work. There are some people who believe it shouldn't work and want to prove it once and for all," said Seattle Mayor Norm Rice, a Democrat.

Rice added there was a third group of pragmatists, he called himself one, that said mayors must figure out how to make the best of the law. He predicted Congress was not likely to make major changes in the next two years.

Rice said he had not given up on finding more money in Congress for transportation and education programs for welfare recipients. At the same time he and other mayors said cities would have to learn to be more innovative with less money.
The welfare law, signed by President Clinton in August, ends a six-decade federal guarantee of aid to poor children. Instead, states will receive block grants to design their own welfare programs.

Benefits will be limited to five years and and most recipients required to find jobs after two years. The law reduces federal spending by $54 billion over six years. Most savings come from cuts in the Food Stamps nutrition program and denying many government benefits to legal immigrants.
Lawmakers who crafted the law worked closely with state governors, who will have broad discretion to design and implement welfare programs. Mayors lobbied against the bill.

The mayors said how the law was implemented was vitally important. States can set more stringent standards than federal law. Mayors want latitude to design broad job training and placement programs, saying they are the ones on the front lines of welfare reform.

Over the past several decades, the incidence of poverty in cities has deepened. At the same time, most new job creation nationwide is not in cities but outlying suburbs making it tough for many mayors to meet work requirement in the law.
"We're going to see those who fall through the cracks and they're not going to be able to fall any further than America's cities," said Patrick Henry Hays, Democratic mayor of North Little Rock, Ark.
Following up, Paul Soglin, Democratic mayor of Madison, Wis., said he was worried that "these cracks are becoming as wide as the Grand Canyon."
